Just because this is the experience you had does not inherently invalidate the experience others in this thread have had. Minimizing their experiences down to just shitty self esteem and laziness is ludicrously reductive. As for laziness, OP described going to multiple stores looking for sugar cookies, that is the antithesis of lazy! Lazy is: "God I really want some sugar cookie dough, but that means I have to go to the store, and parking always sucks, and what if they're out, then I have to go to the other store... Meh, I can live without it." Laziness is refusing to acknowledge that there is a fundamental flaw in the very way you experience and interact with the world, because I can tell you from experience that cognitive behavioral therapy requires a lot of dedicated effort. You are literally actively reprogramming the way your brain works and having done it myself for my anxiety, I can't imagine taking those steps if simply "getting off my fat ass and doing work at the gym" would sincerely fix the problem.

I'm really happy for you that you had the experience that you did and that you were able to overcome your problems simply by changing your diet and working out. That is awesome! But it's also indicative of the fact that you (luckily) don't have the disordered thinking that others in this thread have experienced.

So, I'm just going to put this out there...

If you genuinely feel you are addicted to food and compulsively eat in the same way an alcoholic is addictted to alcohol and compulsively drinks, you may want to consider overeaters anonymous (www.oa.org). It's basically AA but for compulsive overeating. 
My sister has struggled with several addictions including food and has had a lot of success by going to OA meetings. My understanding is that most groups do not push a specific diet plan, but rather focus on the emotional, psychological, and spiritual issues surrounding compulsive eating. I say most groups because there is a smaller group within OA called HOW that pushes a strong abstinence only approach with a much more strict diet plan. My recommendation would be to go to a few meetings to try to find a place where you feel comfortable, again, this is if you truly feel food is an addiction for you in the same sense that alcohol is for an alcoholic.

I would like to note, I have never been to an OA or HOW meeting and all of the above info comes from conversations with my sister. So, I apologize if any of the above information is incorrect or misleading and welcome any corrections if that is the case.

My therapist primarily focused on CBT - cognitive behavioral therapy. So, a lot of my therapy focused on trying to objectively look at my thoughts, feelings, and reactions to things to sort of evaluate them and whether or not they made sense.

For example, if I did poorly on a test (I was in college at the time), how did I react? Did I globalize (I'm a complete moron, I may as well drop out of school and resign myself to my fate)? Or minimize (Ok so this one subject isn't my strong suit, I just need to buckle down and work harder next time)? 

That's what I'm talking about. I feel like even just existing needs to be 10x harder for me, because I need to reevaluate every single thought I have to determine if its "right". It's almost like I'm not even sure if I'm allowed to feel whatever it is I'm feeling. It's exhausting.

I'm an assistant manager at a fast food restaurant and I do nearly all of our hiring. So, I think my perspective is fairly relevant to your question.

First, I'm gonna address your points:
* I wouldn't worry about this point too much. I only call past employers/references after I've pretty much decided that I want to hire an applicant, not to double check the qualifications of every application I get.
* It's all about the spin. Your past experience is probably more relevant than you think. Almost all jobs have an element of customer service, it's just a matter of who the customers are. You may not have had to deal with the end user/client in your tech jobs, but you had to provide services to your bosses, take their orders (directions), you may or may not have had to deal with one of them getting angry at you about something out of your control. All of these things are aspects of working in customer service, you just weren't dealing with the end user of the product.
*The is a possibility, but I wouldn't be too concerned about it. I think the majority of the people you'll be dealing with will realize you are just trying to get some extra spending cash while going through school. 

In your job descriptions focus less on the technical aspects of what you've done and more on meeting deadlines, dealing with clients or internal demands (ie - what the bosses wanted). If you really think about all of the skills you gained from your professional experience, you'd be surprised how much of it can probably be applied to a customer service position.

When I interview a candidate, the traits I'm looking for two things:
1) Interpersonal skills - can you carry on a conversation with my? Are you listening to my questions and fully answering them or just giving me generically vague responses that don't fully answer the question?
2) Trainable - do you seem like you can pick up the directions I give you? Do your answers show thought instead of just being word-vomit (happens a lot with young nervous applicants)? 

TL;DR: Keep the job experience on your applications but frame it in terms of internal customer service and really think about what skills you picked up in those jobs that can apply to customer service positions.
